summary: Describes the general PANA framework, including its functional elements, a high-level call flow, and deployment environments. It gives background for understanding how the protocol is meant to be used. It is informational.

subtitle: The four players in PANA network-access authentication, how they talk, and the two kinds of networks it fits.

tldr.problem: Clients need to be authenticated and authorized before they get network access, on any kind of link and whether or not the network is already physically or cryptographically secured.
tldr.mechanism: PANA carries EAP over IP between a client (PaC) and a server (PAA). The PAA consults an authentication server and tells an enforcement point to open its filters, with an optional secure association step afterward.
tldr.outcome: The framework describes the functional elements, a high-level call flow and two deployment environments. Protocol details live in other documents.

facts.label: PAA to AS protocols
facts.value: RADIUS, Diameter, LDAP or an API

today: RFC 5193 is an Informational RFC from May 2008, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Protocol details are in RFC 5191.

sections.title: What PANA Is
sections.content:
PANA (Protocol for carrying Authentication for Network Access) is a link-layer agnostic network access authentication protocol. It runs between a client that wants network access and a server on the network side, and defines a new EAP lower layer that uses IP between the two endpoints.

Motivation and requirements are in RFC 4058, and protocol details are in RFC 5191. After a successful PANA authentication, per-packet security can come from physical security, link-layer ciphering or IPsec. PANA is meant for any access network, and while a PANA deployment must ensure the integrity of PANA messages when the EAP method produces an MSK, supporting link-layer or network-layer security is not mandatory.
sections.eli5: PANA is a sign-in desk for a network. It works the same no matter which kind of cable or radio you came in through.

sections.title: The Four Functional Entities
sections.content:
A AAA and access control framework using PANA has four entities:

  • PANA Client (PaC): runs on the node requesting access, such as a laptop, PDA, cell phone, desktop PC or router.
  • PANA Authentication Agent (PAA): the PANA server. It consults the authentication server and updates access control state at the enforcement points. It sits on a node typically called a NAS and may be one or more IP hops from the PaCs.
  • Authentication Server (AS): verifies credentials and returns the result with authorization parameters such as allowed bandwidth or IP configuration. It terminates EAP and the EAP methods.
  • Enforcement Point (EP): lets data from authorized clients through and drops the rest, using filters at the link or IP layer.

The PAA and AS usually talk with a protocol such as RADIUS or Diameter, or an API if they share a node. Entities may be colocated: for example the PAA and EP on the same node in DSL networks, or the PAA and AS on one access router in small enterprises. Those choices are deployment decisions outside the document.
sections.eli5: There is a visitor, a front-desk clerk, a records office that checks the visitor's ID, and a door guard who only lets approved visitors in.

sections.title: The Call Flow
sections.content:
An unauthorized client may send only limited traffic, such as PANA, DHCP and router discovery, so it can still take part in PANA. The PaC configures an IP address before running PANA, for instance a link-local one, and may reconfigure or add addresses after success. General-purpose applications cannot use the interface until PANA succeeds.

The PaC discovers the PAA, then runs the EAP exchange over PANA while the PAA talks to the AS. The PAA reports the result to the PaC. On success it sends PaC-specific attributes, such as IP address and keys, to the EP using another protocol, and the EP changes its filters. If cryptographic access control is needed, a secure association protocol runs between the PaC and EP, using parameters derived from the PANA authentication. Per-packet protection adds overhead only between the PaC and EP.
sections.eli5: The visitor shows ID at the desk, the clerk checks with the records office, and then the guard is told to let that visitor through.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Networks
sections.content:
The RFC separates networks by when the secure channel exists.

Secure channel before PANA. Protection against spoofing and eavesdropping already exists, yet user authentication is still required. Examples are a DSL network protected by physical wiring and a cdma2000 network with link-layer ciphering already enabled. No secure association step is needed after PANA, and the EAP method choice depends on this existing security.

Secure channel created after PANA. There is no lower-layer protection first, so PANA runs on a channel open to eavesdropping and spoofing. The EAP method must resist those attacks and must create cryptographic keys for the later secure association protocol. Choosing link-layer or network-layer per-packet security is a deployment decision. With IP-layer protection the protocol would be IKE and the protection IPsec AH/ESP.
sections.eli5: Some buildings already have locked hallways before you reach the desk. In others, you only get a key after you sign in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says security is discussed throughout the document. For protocol-specific security considerations it points to RFC 4016 and RFC 5191.
sections.eli5: The safety rules are written in other documents, and this one points you to them.
